title: CI/CD for Automation (GitHub Actions)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# CI/CD for Automation (GitHub Actions) ##### The deploy that took the client's automations offline for six hours An agency's deployment process was a wiki page: run the tests locally, build the Docker image, push it, SSH to the server, pull, restart. Seven manual steps, followed most of the time. On a Friday, an engineer skipped the test step — a one-line config change, obviously safe. The change renamed an environment variable the n8n workers read. Main started fine. Workers crash-looped. Because nobody watched the rollout after the restart, the failure went unnoticed until Monday, and six hours of client webhooks had been rejected. Systematic reviews of continuous delivery practice (Shahin et al., 2017) consistently identify the same root cause: **manual, undocumented, inconsistently executed deployment steps**. The fix is not discipline. It is removing the opportunity for a human to skip a step. ##### The pipeline shape A CI/CD pipeline for automation work has five stages, and each is a gate: ```text push / PR → lint + type-check → test → build image → deploy staging ↓ manual approval → deploy production ``` The principle is **fail fast and cheap**: linting takes 15 seconds and catches trivial problems; the full test suite takes 3 minutes; building and pushing an image takes 5. Ordering them cheapest-first means a formatting error costs you 15 seconds, not 8 minutes. ##### Continuous integration ```yaml # .github/workflows/ci.yml name: CI on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] concurrency: # cancel superseded runs on the same branch group: ci-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: true jobs: quality: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3 with: { enable-cache: true } - run: uv sync --all-extras - run: uv run ruff check . - run: uv run ruff format --check . - run: uv run mypy src/ test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest needs: quality strategy: fail-fast: false matrix: python: ["3.11", "3.12"] # matrix build across versions services: # real dependencies, not mocks postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine env: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test POSTGRES_DB: test options: >- --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 10s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 5 ports: ["5432:5432"] redis: image: redis:7-alpine options: --health-cmd "redis-cli ping" --health-interval 10s ports: ["6379:6379"] env: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5432/test REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379/0 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: ${{ matrix.python }} cache: pip - run: pip install -e ".[dev]" - run: pytest --cov=src --cov-report=xml --cov-fail-under=75 - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 if: always() with: { name: coverage-${{ matrix.python }}, path: coverage.xml } prompt-evals: # automation-specific: catch LLM drift runs-on: ubuntu-latest needs: quality if: contains(github.event.pull_request.changed_files, 'prompts/') steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: pip install -e ".[dev]" - run: python -m evals.run --min-accuracy 0.90 env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY_EVAL }} ``` Three details worth stealing. **`services:`** spins up real Postgres and Redis containers, so tests exercise actual SQL and actual queue behaviour rather than mocks. **`concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress`** stops five queued runs piling up when you push three times in a minute. And the **prompt-evals job** is the automation-specific addition — running your LLM evaluation set in CI is what turns "the model changed and nobody noticed for four days" into a failing check. ##### Building and pushing images ```yaml # .github/workflows/cd.yml name: CD on: push: branches: [main] tags: ["v*"] permissions: contents: read packages: write id-token: write # for OIDC cloud auth — no long-lived keys jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - id: meta uses: docker/metadata-action@v5 with: images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/api tags: | type=sha,prefix=,format=short type=ref,event=tag type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}} - id: push uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }} labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }} cache-from: type=gha # reuse layers across CI runs cache-to: type=gha,mode=max provenance: true ``` The `type=sha` tag is the important one: **every image is tagged with the commit that built it**, so a rollback is unambiguous and you can always answer "what code is running in production?" `cache-from`/`cache-to: type=gha` reuses Docker layers between runs, typically cutting build time by 60–80% — and it works properly only if your Dockerfile orders layers correctly, which is where yesterday's material pays off. ##### Deploying, with an approval gate **GitHub Environments** provide the approval mechanism, scoped secrets and deployment history. ```yaml deploy-staging: needs: build runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: staging url: https://staging.example.com steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v4 - name: Configure cluster access run: echo "${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_STAGING }}" | base64 -d > /tmp/kubeconfig - name: Roll out env: { KUBECONFIG: /tmp/kubeconfig } run: | kubectl set image deployment/automation-api \ api=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/api:${{ github.sha }} kubectl rollout status deployment/automation-api --timeout=180s - name: Smoke test run: | curl -fsS --retry 8 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors \ https://staging.example.com/healthz/ready deploy-production: needs: deploy-staging runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: production # ← protection rules live on the environment url: https://api.example.com steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v4 - run: echo "${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_PROD }}" | base64 -d > /tmp/kubeconfig - name: Roll out env: { KUBECONFIG: /tmp/kubeconfig } run: | kubectl set image deployment/automation-api \ api=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/api:${{ github.sha }} kubectl rollout status deployment/automation-api --timeout=300s - name: Verify or roll back env: { KUBECONFIG: /tmp/kubeconfig } run: | if ! curl -fsS --retry 6 --retry-delay 5 https://api.example.com/healthz/ready; then echo "Smoke test failed — rolling back" kubectl rollout undo deployment/automation-api exit 1 fi ``` The approval gate is **not in the YAML** — it is configured on the environment in repository settings: *Required reviewers*, optional *wait timer*, and *deployment branch* restrictions. The job pauses before its first step until a named reviewer approves, and GitHub records who approved what. The automatic rollback in the final step is what makes unattended deployment safe: if the smoke test fails, the previous version is restored before anyone reads the notification. ##### Secrets and OIDC **Repository secrets** are the baseline. **Environment secrets** are better: staging and production hold different values under the same name, so the workflow does not branch on environment. The stronger pattern is **OIDC federation** — GitHub issues a short-lived token that your cloud provider trusts, eliminating long-lived credentials entirely: ```yaml - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-deploy aws-region: ap-south-1 # no AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY anywhere ``` This is worth adopting as soon as you deploy to a cloud provider. A leaked long-lived key is an incident; a 15-minute OIDC token scoped to one role is not. Rules that still apply: never `echo` a secret, mask anything derived from one, prefer `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` with minimal `permissions:` over a personal access token, and remember that secrets are unavailable to workflows triggered by `pull_request` from forks — by design. ##### Workflow-as-code: promoting n8n and Make This is the automation-specific piece, and it closes the loop on Day 28 of the beginner track. **n8n Source Control** (Git-backed) lets you push workflows from a development instance to a branch and pull them into production. That turns workflow promotion into a pull request — reviewable, revertible, and auditable. Where Source Control is unavailable, export via the CLI and commit: ```yaml promote-n8n: runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Import workflows into production n8n run: | for f in workflows/n8n/*.json; do curl -fsS -X POST "$N8N_URL/api/v1/workflows" \ -H "X-N8N-API-KEY: $N8N_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data-binary "@$f" done env: N8N_URL: ${{ secrets.N8N_URL }} N8N_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.N8N_API_KEY }} ``` Add a **secret-scanning gate** before any workflow JSON is committed, because exported workflows occasionally contain a credential someone typed directly into a node: ```yaml - name: Scan exported workflows for secrets run: | if grep -rEi '"(api[_-]?key|token|password|secret)"\s*:\s*"[^"]{12,}"' workflows/; then echo "::error::Possible credential in exported workflow" exit 1 fi ``` Publishing a **custom n8n node to npm** fits the same pattern, triggered on tags: ```yaml publish-node: if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: { node-version: 20, registry-url: https://registry.npmjs.org } - run: npm ci && npm run build && npm test - run: npm publish --access public env: NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }} ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Push / PR] --> B[Lint + mypy
15s] B --> C[Tests + coverage
matrix, real services] C --> D[Prompt evals
if prompts changed] D --> E[Build + push image
tagged with SHA] E --> F[Deploy staging
+ smoke test] F --> G{{Manual approval
required reviewer}} G --> H[Deploy production] H --> I{Smoke test?} I -->|pass| J[Notify success] I -->|fail| K[kubectl rollout undo
+ alert] ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **No approval gate** on production. - **Deploying `:latest`** — untraceable and unrollbackable. - **No smoke test after deploy**, so a broken rollout looks successful. - **No automatic rollback** on smoke-test failure. - **Secrets echoed** into logs. - **Long-lived cloud credentials** instead of OIDC. - **No caching**, making every CI run slow enough that people bypass it. - **Tests against mocks only**, missing real SQL and queue behaviour. - **No concurrency control**, causing overlapping deploys of different commits. - **Migrations run inside the app container** on startup, so N replicas race to migrate — run them as a separate pre-deploy job. - **Committing exported workflows without scanning** for embedded credentials. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a pipeline that **lints, tests, builds a Docker image, and deploys on merge to main**, with a **required manual approval gate** for production. Then test the gate by merging something and watching the run pause — and check that the deployment appears in the repository's Environments tab with your approval recorded. The mini project is that pipeline for your **FastAPI service** end to end. Add the two automation-specific jobs while you are there: the prompt-eval gate and the workflow-JSON secret scan. Both take ten minutes and both prevent categories of incident described earlier in this course. For the assignment, **add a production environment with a required approval before deploy**, and document the protection rules you configured — required reviewers, branch restrictions, and any wait timer. Then deliberately break the smoke test and confirm the automatic rollback fires. A pipeline whose failure path you have never exercised is a pipeline you should not trust. ##### Key takeaways - Order pipeline stages cheapest-first, and make every stage a gate: lint, type-check, test against real services, build, deploy. - Tag every image with the commit SHA so deployments are traceable and rollbacks unambiguous; use registry layer caching to keep builds fast. - GitHub Environments provide approval gates, scoped secrets and deployment history — the approval lives in settings, not the YAML. - Prefer OIDC federation over long-lived cloud credentials, and keep `permissions:` minimal on every workflow. - Treat exported n8n/Make workflows as versioned artifacts promoted through pull requests, scan them for embedded credentials, and run prompt evaluations in CI to catch model drift.
